policies.name: AI Usage
description: AI, like any technology, carries risks and benefits. It is to your advantage to understand both clearly.

Risks: Heavy, unreflective AI use is linked to cognitive offloading. Research suggests that relying on AI to produce answers, rather than to support your own reasoning, can reduce engagement with the thinking process itself and may weaken independent problem-solving over time.
[1] [2] [3] [4]

Benefits: When used as a Socratic partner, debugger, or explainer rather than an answer generator, AI has been shown to improve critical thinking, argumentation, and conceptual understanding. Students who actively critique AI output rather than accepting it at face value tend to learn more than students who simply defer to it.
[1] [2] [3] [4]

Learning to use AI well is a valuable skill, but it cannot replace your independent reasoning, judgment, and creativity. While companies use AI to automate routine knowledge work, human value lies in the ability to critique these tools, know when to question them, and go beyond what they can produce. This class is your opportunity to develop those unique, non-automated strengths. Ultimately, your worth is not defined by economic productivity or outperforming a machine. Rather, the goal for this class is to cultivate a deep conceptual understanding and human agency that algorithms will struggle to replicate.
All work you turn in is expected to be your own. In order to earn full points on assessments, you must be able to fully and clearly explain all aspects of your work.

instructions.Presentations:
Students will work on a term project throughout the semester and present that project over three talks.

Deliverable

By Sunday evening of the week of a presentation, students should submit their project in its most recent state as a single compressed (.zip) email attachment to the instructor.

Talk

Each talk will feature two primary, interwoven components:
  1. Demo. Prepared demonstration / explanation. The student prepares this ahead of time. Counts towards the grade.
  2. QnA. Dynamic question answering. Instructor initiated at various points during the demo. Student response assessed and considered toward grade assignment.

Students will be in front of the class for equivalent amounts of time during each presentation. What will vary between students is the amount of time spent on demo versus QnA. Demos that are informative and engaging will likely involve / necessitate less QnA, so it is in a student's best interest to make the demo portion(s) as informative and engaging as possible.

Durations

Presentation Duration
1: The Pitch 5 min
2: The Progress 5 min
3: The...Perfection? 5 min


Rubric

2 pts 1 pt 0 pts
Deliverable truency On time. Late, or deliverable not submitted.
Deliverable progress At or exceeding. Some work, but lagging. Well behind, or deliverable not submitted.
Demo representation Totally matches deliverable. Somewhat matches deliverable. Doesn't match deliverable, or deliverable not submitted.
Demo clarity Very clear. Somewhat clear. Not clear.
Demo engagement Very engaging Somewhat engaging. Not engaging.
QnA accuracy Answers fully correct. Partially but mostly correct. Frequently incorrect responses.
QnA clarity Answers completely clear. Mostly but not entirely clear. Answers pretty unclear.
QnA ownership Definitive ownership. Somewhat questionable ownership. Highly questionable ownership.


Notes

  1. Time limits are firm. Practice with a timer.
  2. Presentation order will be randomly determined by instructor ahead of time.
  3. Have a plan B for demo failures (recording, second machine, etc). Recovering well counts.
  4. Slides/notecards fine. Scripts and pre-loaded AI answers are not.
instructions.Lab reports:
Download the lab report template (PDF, 2 pages)

Print one copy of the template for each lab, double-sided on a single sheet, and fill it out by hand, during the lab period. Everything for a lab is done in the lab: nothing is taken home or finished later, and the sheet is due on paper before you leave. Legibility and presentation are important and will be graded. The report records what you and your Pico actually did today, not what the lesson says should happen. Each lab page ends with a Your Lab Report Sheet section that says what goes in each part of the sheet for that lab.

Front: where you write

  1. Head. Lab number, your name, your lab partner(s), and the date.
  2. Goal. What today’s lab is meant to accomplish, in your own words.
  3. Check-off tests / drills. One row per test or drill, numbered as on the lab page. Where the lab asks for a prediction, write it before you run the test. Then write what actually happened (numbers, counts, observations), mark pass or fail, and get the instructor’s initials when you show it working.
  4. MicroPython code. The lines you wrote or changed, not the whole file and not code copied from the lesson. Write the file name, then one statement per numbered line. The dotted guides mark four-space indents, so keep your indentation straight.
  5. Measured or observed. Real values from your own system: readings, timings, counts, message rates. Not numbers copied from the lesson.
  6. What went wrong. What failed, how you found the cause, and how you fixed it. If you did not finish, say exactly where you got stuck. Short questions at the end of each lab are answered here too.

Back: wiring and parts

  1. The back is a full page for your wiring. Turn the sheet 90° clockwise to read it: every label is then upright. It shows a breadboard with the Pico WH seated across the centre channel, pins in columns c and h, as you build it in lab, with every Pico pin labeled.
  2. Around the breadboard are the parts used across the course: sensors and inputs on one side, outputs, power and passives on the other. Each part has its pins drawn as short stubs. Extend the pins you use with a line to a breadboard hole or a Pico pin.
  3. Write the Pico pin and any resistor value on each wire. For a lab with little or no new wiring, sketch the message flow between your nodes in the margins instead.

Notes

  1. Write it as you go, not afterward. Notes made live are worth more than a tidy copy made later.
  2. Honesty is valued. A test or drill you could not make work, with a good account of why, scores better than a made-up result.
  3. Specific detail that shows meaningful understanding is essential to earn full points, not vague descriptions or padded length.
  4. Sketches and arrows are welcome. Neat is better than pretty.
